Burundi is a small, crowded country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, on the north-east shore of Lake Tanganyika. The map shows it from 1815 to the present, first as an independent kingdom and later as a colony and republic.

The Kingdom of Burundi was founded around the late 1600s and ruled by a king, the mwami, for over two centuries. As in neighbouring Rwanda, its people were Hutu, Tutsi and Twa, but the princes of the royal line, the ganwa, held power as a group of their own.

Germany made Burundi part of German East Africa in the 1890s. After the First World War, Belgium took it over as part of Ruanda-Urundi, ruling through the Tutsi elite and hardening ethnic divisions.

Burundi became independent in 1962 as a kingdom; the army abolished the monarchy in 1966. The Tutsi-led army and Hutu rebels then clashed again and again:

  • In 1972 the army killed a large number of Hutu, perhaps 100,000 or more, after a Hutu uprising.
  • In 1993 the first elected Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, was murdered months after taking office, and a civil war began that lasted until about 2005.

A peace deal signed at Arusha in 2000 shared power between Hutu and Tutsi, and Pierre Nkurunziza, a former Hutu rebel, became president in 2005. His bid for a third term in 2015 set off a new crisis. Burundi remains one of the poorest countries in the world.
sum: Burundi is a small, crowded country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, on the north-east shore of Lake Tanganyika. The map shows it from 1815 to the present, first as an independent kingdom and later as a colony and republic.
